blocks.text: Pneumothorax is the abnormal accumulation of air within the pleural cavity, resulting in partial or complete collapse of the affected lung due to loss of the normal negative intrapleural pressure.
Normally, the intrapleural pressure is negative relative to atmospheric pressure, keeping the lungs expanded against the chest wall.
When air enters the pleural space, this pressure relationship is disrupted, resulting in lung collapse.

Primary spontaneous pneumothorax
Occurs without clinically apparent underlying lung disease. It is commonly associated with rupture of subpleural blebs or bullae.
Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax
Occurs in the presence of underlying lung disease.
Important causes:
A. Simple pneumothorax
Air accumulates in the pleural cavity, causing partial or complete lung collapse without significant mediastinal compression or circulatory compromise.
B. Tension pneumothorax
A life-threatening condition in which progressive air accumulation increases intrathoracic pressure, compresses the affected lung and reduces venous return to the heart.
This can cause obstructive shock and cardiac arrest.
C. Open pneumothorax
Air enters the pleural cavity through an open chest wall defect.
D. Occult pneumothorax
A pneumothorax not visible on the initial supine chest X-ray but detected on CT or other imaging.

blocks.title: The mechanism involves a one-way valve effect:

items.text: Air enters the pleural cavity during inspiration.
Air cannot escape adequately during expiration.
The mediastinum may shift towards the opposite side.
The vena cava and other intrathoracic structures become compressed.
Obstructive shock and cardiac arrest may occur.

blocks.text: Clinical pearl: Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis. Treatment must not be delayed for chest X-ray confirmation in an unstable patient.
The diagnosis is based on clinical assessment and imaging, except in suspected tension pneumothorax with haemodynamic instability, where immediate treatment takes priority.

Pneumothorax is air in the pleural cavity.
Primary spontaneous pneumothorax occurs without clinically apparent underlying lung disease.
Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax occurs in patients with underlying lung disease.
COPD is an important cause of secondary spontaneous pneumothorax.
Tracheal deviation is a late and unreliable sign of tension pneumothorax.
Hyperresonance and reduced breath sounds are classical examination findings.
The pleural line with absent peripheral lung markings is the classical chest X-ray finding.
Lung point is a highly specific ultrasound sign.
Finger thoracostomy is an effective emergency decompression technique when performed by trained clinicians.
Definitive treatment of tension pneumothorax is chest tube drainage.
VATS with bullectomy and/or pleurodesis reduces recurrence.
Persistent air leak requires thoracic specialist assessment.
A stable, minimally symptomatic primary spontaneous pneumothorax can sometimes be managed conservatively irrespective of size.
Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax generally requires more cautious management.
Routine antibiotics are not indicated in uncomplicated spontaneous pneumothorax.
Patients should not fly until complete radiological resolution and the recommended waiting period.
